Booking Holdings — unit economics (room nights, gross bookings, take rate)

BKNG-unit-econ-2026-09-24 · USD · series 2026-09-24T23:40:00Z · built 2026-09-25 01:31 UTC

The short version

Booking prints a clear operating scoreboard every quarter: how many room nights were booked, how much dollar volume those bookings represent (gross bookings), and how revenue splits between merchant, agency, and advertising. Those numbers live in the earnings release. Latest locked quarter (second quarter 2026): 325 million room nights, $51.0 billion gross bookings, of which about $37.0 billion merchant and $14.0 billion agency. Revenue was $7.35 billion, so the take rate (revenue divided by gross bookings) was about 14.4%. Gross bookings per room night were about $157. Income and the trailing multiple stay on the key-metrics page.

Booking Desk · Latent capital · as of the quarter ended June 30, 2026

What Booking prints

Printed as levels:

  • Room nights (millions)
  • Gross bookings — total, and usually merchant versus agency
  • Revenue split — merchant revenues, agency revenues, advertising and other revenues
  • Often also: rental car days, flight tickets
  • In recent releases: marketing expense as a percent of gross bookings

Not printed as absolute levels: room nights, gross bookings, or revenue by geography. Company-wide constant-currency growth appears. Regional levels do not. Those absolute stacks stay blank.

Room nights and gross bookings

Room nights recovered from the 2020 trough and have kept growing into 2026. The second quarter of 2026 was 325 million nights, up about 5% year over year.

Full-year 2025, as printed in the year release, was about 1,235 million room nights. Full-year 2024 was about 1,144 million. The year view runs from 2015 through 2025. Hatched years, 2015 through 2022, are the four quarters added together. 2023 through 2025 are the company’s own year print.

Gross bookings in the second quarter of 2026 were $51.0 billion, up about 9% as reported. Full-year 2025 gross bookings were $186.1 billion, against $165.6 billion in 2024.

Year-over-year growth in room nights and gross bookings is drawn once a year-ago quarter exists. The second quarter of 2026 was about 5% for nights and about 9% for gross bookings. Quarters before that lag are left off the line.

Who collects the money

The model has been moving steadily toward merchant. Merchant’s share of gross bookings was roughly a quarter in mid-2019 and about three-quarters by the second quarter of 2026 (about 26% to about 73%). Agency gross bookings have declined in absolute terms in recent years even as the total grew. Of the $51.0 billion booked in the second quarter of 2026, $37.0 billion was merchant and $14.0 billion was agency.

The line below is that share, merchant bookings divided by the total.

The same shift shows up in revenue. For the second quarter of 2026, merchant revenue was about $5.13 billion, agency about $1.90 billion, and advertising and other about $322 million, totaling $7.35 billion — the same revenue as the income statement for the quarter.

What Booking keeps

Take rate here means revenue divided by gross bookings for the same period, only where both exist. It is seasonal: first quarters run lower (roughly 10% recently), third quarters higher (high teens), with second and fourth quarters typically mid-teens. The second quarter of 2026 was about 14.4%. A year earlier the same quarter was about 14.6%. Full-year 2025 was about 14.5%. Across the full history the range is wide because 2020 and 2021 were not a normal year. Where either revenue or gross bookings is missing, the ratio is left blank.

A trailing-twelve-month take rate — four quarters of revenue divided by four quarters of gross bookings — sits around 14.3% as of the second quarter of 2026. It is steadier than the seasonal quarterly ratio.

Gross bookings per room night were about $157 in the second quarter of 2026. It is a rough check on price, mix, and currency in the booking pool. It is not an average daily rate.

Marketing as a percent of gross bookings, when Booking prints it, has recently been around 3.8% to 4.7%. The second quarter of 2026 was 4.7%. The chart starts in the fourth quarter of 2024. Earlier quarters are omitted. They are not filled in.

Flight tickets and rental-car days are printed in the same table as room nights. In the second quarter of 2026 Booking printed 17 million flight tickets and 23 million rental-car days.

How fast the income line is growing

For the quarter ended June 30, 2026, revenue was up about 8% year over year and about 33% from the prior quarter. Net income was up about 118% year over year and about 80% from the prior quarter — a wide swing that is as much about the prior-year base as about run-rate. The chart is the year-over-year change. It starts in the first quarter of 2016, when a year-ago quarter first exists. Gross profit growth is not on the chart. Booking stopped reporting a usable single-quarter gross profit after 2017, and this dig does not invent one.

Where the map stops

This dig does not claim a regional stack of room nights or gross bookings. The earnings tables are company totals. Constant-currency growth is printed for the whole company. Absolute Europe, Asia, or Americas levels stay blank. A growth rate is not turned into an invented regional dollar.

The share of Booking.com room nights that are alternative accommodations is not printed as a level. Average daily rate is not printed as a dollar level. Adjusted EBITDA is not in this dig. Income levels and the trailing multiple stay on the key-metrics page. There is no price on this page.

Why this matters

Trailing earnings and income levels are already on the key-metrics page. Unit economics add three handles that do not require a new multiple:

  1. Take rate — how much of each booking dollar becomes revenue.
  2. Gross bookings per room night — a rough check on pricing, mix, and currency in the booking pool.
  3. Marketing as a percent of gross bookings — how much of the booking dollar is spent to generate demand, when printed.

Together with the merchant-mix shift, they frame whether growth is coming from more nights, higher spend per night, a richer take, or a different collection model.
